references.text: Matthew's parallel account where Jesus says that any kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and that a city or house divided against itself cannot stand.

Mark's parallel account where Jesus uses the same argument: a kingdom divided against itself cannot endure, a house divided against itself cannot endure, and Satan cannot stand if he rises up against himself.
The immediate context: some accused Jesus of casting out demons by Beelzebul, while others tested him by demanding a sign from heaven. Verse 17 is Jesus' response to this accusation.
Isaiah prophesies about Egypt where the Lord will stir Egyptian against Egyptian, so that they fight each other—an example of a kingdom divided from within and laid waste.
Daniel describes God's kingdom as one that shatters all other kingdoms, in contrast to kingdoms that fall—relevant to the theme of the endurance and collapse of kingdoms.
The earth was full of violence and all flesh had corrupted its way—an example from the Old Testament showing that internal corruption leads to destruction.
Paul warns the Galatians: if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by each other—an echo of Jesus' principle that internal division leads to ruin.
Jesus follows up by applying the principle directly to Satan: if Satan has risen up against himself, how then can his kingdom stand?
He who troubles his own house shall inherit wind—a proverb that underscores the same principle that internal division leads to destruction.
Jesus knew their thoughts—just as in 11:17 he knew what they were thinking (εἰδὼς αὐτῶν τὰ διανοήματα), this shows Jesus' supernatural knowledge of human thoughts.
Jesus did not need anyone to testify about man, for he himself knew what was in man—parallel to his knowing their thoughts in Luke 11:17.
